title: You did it: from first print to real problem-solver
idea: GUIDED FINALE & CELEBRATION. Reflect on the whole journey, confirm the solving method you now own, and take the next step: writing real code in a real editor.
problem: The final 'problem': recognize everything you can now do, and plan your next move as a real programmer.

exercises.prompt: This is the very last lesson. First, Understand how far you've come. What can you now do that you couldn't at lesson one?
options: Read a problem, plan it, write code, and check it myself
exercises.explanation: You started with print() and now you solve unseen problems end to end. That's the leap from typing to THINKING like a programmer.

exercises.prompt: What is the method you'll carry into every future problem?
exercises.explanation: UEPCC is yours now. Name the I/O, work an example, plan the steps, write code, check against the example. It works on any problem.

exercises.prompt: Example — your toolkit. Which of these have you actually used in these capstones?
options: Variables, if/else, loops, lists, and functions
exercises.explanation: All of them, woven together. FizzBuzz, digit sums, filters, stats reports, your own functions — real programs.

exercises.prompt: You can now solve a problem you've never seen before by breaking it into small, known steps.
exercises.explanation: Yes! That's the whole skill. New problems aren't scary when you decompose them into pieces you already know.

exercises.prompt: Plan your next step beyond this course. Order a sensible path.
blocks: Install Python and open a real code editor
Type a small program you plan with UEPCC
Run it, see real output, and iterate
exercises.explanation: Move from these guided exercises to a real editor. Set up Python, write a planned program, run it, and improve it. That's real coding.

exercises.prompt: When you face your first real-editor program, what's the wise first move?
options: Plan it with UEPCC before typing
Copy a huge program you don't understand
exercises.explanation: Plan first, always. The method that carried you through these capstones is exactly what professionals use on new problems.

exercises.prompt: You're ready to write real code. In an editor, which line prints a greeting — the very first thing you ever learned?
exercises.explanation: print("Hello, world!") — where you began, and now just one small tool among many you command. Full circle!

exercises.prompt:
Write that classic first line of a real program:

____("Hello, world!")
exercises.explanation: print — your first tool and still a trusty one. The difference now: you know what to put AROUND it to solve real problems.

exercises.prompt: Check your readiness: a friend asks you to count how many numbers in a list are even. Can you solve it?
options: Yes — loop the list, test item % 2 == 0, count the matches
exercises.explanation: You've got this — count-with-condition, built by hand. You can genuinely solve problems now. That's real.

exercises.prompt: Final check of the whole journey: you went from print() to planning, looping, listing, and writing functions. What's true?
options: I'm a beginning programmer now, ready to write real code
exercises.explanation: Congratulations! You can read a problem, plan it, code it, and check it. Open a real editor and build something. This is the beginning, not the end. Well done!
